title: Diffusion Transformers are Provably Optimal In-context Generators

paper.title: Diffusion Transformers are Provably Optimal In-context Generators
paper.abstract: Abstract Generative foundation models are attracting interest for their ability to produce desired outputs from demonstrations given at inference time, without updating parameters. However, since a few demonstrations cannot uniquely identify the intended task, the challenge is how to learn and sample from an output distribution that reflects this task uncertainty. In this work, we theoretically analyze how a Diffusion Transformer (DiT), pretrained across diverse tasks, learns and generates predictive distributions for a new query from demonstrations. We first show that the natural target to generate from finite demonstrations is not an output derived from estimating a single task, but rather a predictive distribution that captures the task uncertainty remaining after observing the demonstrations. We then prove that a DiT can learn this predictive distribution through score estimation, using attention to aggregate information from demonstrations and diffusion to generate samples. Owing to this property, with sufficient pretraining resources and diffusion sampling steps, the resulting DiT achieves the minimax optimal rate over a Hölder class of test-time tasks. These results imply that DiT acts as a statistically grounded in-context generator capable of generating distributions adapted to new tasks while retaining the uncertainty inherent in finite demonstrations.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Generative models have advanced rapidly over the past few years with diffusion models in particular achieving remarkable success in synthesizing complex high-dimensional data such as images ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Chi et al., 2023 ) . At the same time, in-context learning (ICL) has shown that a pretrained model can adapt to a new task from a few demonstrations without updating its parameters ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Dong et al., 2024 ) . These developments motivate in-context generation : using demonstrations to specify what kinds of outputs should be generated for a new query ( Bar et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) . Fig. 1 illustrates this idea in a robotic manipulation example: a user provides several examples of acceptable behaviors and asks the model to generate an appropriate action for a new object. More broadly, in image generation and other structured domains ( Fu et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) , the desired behavior may depend on visual, geometric, or stylistic criteria that are cumbersome to specify perfectly in natural language or mathematical form. In such cases, demonstrations serve as a natural interface for specifying what should be generated, and in-context generation is the mechanism that turns this interface into a working system. Yet demonstrations are not necessarily a complete specification of the underlying task. With only finitely many examples, multiple latent rules may remain compatible with the same context while implying different outputs for a new query, leaving uncertainty about what should be generated ( Xie et al., 2022 ; Panwar et al., 2024 ) . The output distribution that the context induces at a new query is then frequently non-degenerate or even multimodal. Collapsing this distribution to its mean can yield implausible outputs (Fig. 1 ; see also Blau and Michaeli, 2018 ; Chi et al., 2023 ). Selecting a single plausible candidate instead discards the relative probabilities of alternatives, preventing faithful reproduction of the distribution and potentially compromising downstream decision-making under uncertainty ( Kohl et al., 2018 ; Hoeting et al., 1999 ; Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ) . Thus, what in-context generation should deliver is not a single prediction but samples drawn from the predictive distribution itself, so that the uncertainty left by the finite demonstrations is preserved. Figure 1: In-context generation from demonstrations. A user specifies a desired behavior through a few examples rather than an explicit rule. Because a finite context may be consistent with multiple underlying rules, different outputs can remain plausible for the same query; collapsing the plausible outputs to a single average can produce an invalid result. Despite substantial theoretical progress on both in-context learning and diffusion models, existing frameworks do not cover this generative setting. Most finite-sample statistical analyses of ICL focus on point prediction under regression-type losses, studying how pretrained Transformers output optimal regression rules or Bayes predictors from a finite context ( Bai et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Wakayama and Suzuki, 2026 ) . In contrast, conditional generative modeling and conditional diffusion models aim to learn an entire output distribution given an observed covariate or conditioning variable ( Fu et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2025 ) . These settings typically assume that, at the population level, the observed condition indexes a well-defined conditional distribution. In-context generation is different: the condition itself is a finite collection of demonstrations generated from an unobserved task, and provides only partial information about the test distribution. Consequently, it remains unclear how a predictive distribution should be formed from finitely many demonstrations, and how a pretrained generative model can learn and sample from this distribution across tasks. In this paper, we formulate in-context generation as sampling from the distribution of outputs that remain plausible after finite demonstrations, rather than committing to a single inferred task or output. We identify this target with the posterior-predictive distribution and give a finite-sample theory of how a pretrained diffusion Transformer ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 , DiT;) learns the corresponding prompt-to-distribution map and realizes it through diffusion sampling. Our main findings are as follows. • Pretraining learns the shared rule; demonstrations reduce task uncertainty. We identify two distinct error sources: error from learning and sampling the shared prompt-to-distribution mapping, and the uncertainty left by the current prompt. More pretraining data and computation can reduce the former, but cannot in general eliminate the latter. • Attention infers; diffusion generates. Our construction shows that attention aggregates evidence from demonstrations into weights over plausible tasks, while diffusion converts the resulting predictive mixture into samples. With finite pretraining data and no task labels, a sufficiently large DiT and sampler can approximate the posterior-predictive distribution to any prescribed accuracy under our assumptions. • Minimax-optimal in-context generation via DiT. We establish matching upper and lower bounds for finite-prompt uncertainty and show that, over the nondegenerate Hölder task class, the learned DiT attains the minimax-optimal prompt-length rate log ⁡ n / n \sqrt{\log n/n} in task-conditional total-variation error, given sufficient model capacity, pretraining episodes, and diffusion steps. This demonstrates the test-time adaptive generation of DiT. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 defines the data-generating process and evaluation criteria, then introduces the DiT, its training objective, and its reverse sampler. Section 3 explains the task-family assumptions and the score-learning, prompt-uncertainty, and task-conditional generation guarantees, together with the main ideas behind their proofs. Section 4 presents a summary and practical implications. The appendices contain the proofs and empirical illustrations.

sections.heading: 1.1 Related Work
sections.text: (A) ICL theory. Existing statistical theories of ICL primarily study point prediction, often under regression-type losses, and characterize how pretrained Transformers implement or approximate task-adaptive estimators ( Bai et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024b ; Kim et al., 2024 ) . Bayesian analyses further interpret ICL through posterior prediction over latent tasks ( Wakayama and Suzuki, 2026 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . Our focus is different: we study generation of the full posterior-predictive output distribution and its finite-sample error under distributional loss. Kang et al. (2026) give a constructive Transformer approximation of the posterior-predictive distribution in Gaussian-process (GP) regression. However, their theory assumes a known GP model with fixed kernel and noise parameters and does not establish generalization from finite pretraining data. By contrast, our result learns a prompt-conditioned diffusion score from finitely many independent pretraining examples without knowing the Hölder task family or task prior, and controls expected posterior-predictive TV error of the resulting finite-step reverse diffusion sampler. (B) Score learning with Transformers. Prior work shows Transformers can represent score estimators or denoising updates ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Smart et al., 2025 ; Rosu et al., 2025 ) ; Adibi et al. (2026) construct frozen Transformers simulating closed-form diffusion recursions and approximating an estimation-free empirical sampler. Our focus is statistical rather than merely representational: we analyze a DiT learned from finite pretraining data and show that finite-step reverse diffusion achieves posterior-predictive accuracy, achieving the minimax-optimal rate with respect to prompt length. Further related work on diffusion model theory is discussed in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 2 In-Context Generation Setup and Diffusion Transformer
sections.text: We first specify the data-generating process and the two output distributions used to evaluate in-context generation. We then introduce the prompt-conditioned Diffusion Transformer, its training objective, and its reverse diffusion sampler. The task-family assumptions used to prove the guarantees are stated separately in Section 3 . Appendix B gives the formal probability conventions.

sections.heading: 3.2 A sharp information rate from finite prompts at test time
sections.text: A sharp rate for prompt-based generation. A finite prompt can leave several task-specific output distributions consistent with the demonstrations. The next result gives the sharp worst-case task-conditional accuracy available to any prompt-based generator. The lower bound lets the generator know the full task family and prior and includes generation randomness in its output distribution. Theorem 3.2 (Sharp finite-prompt rate; informal version of Theorem H.1 ) . Under Assumption 3.1 , the following statements hold. • Uniform upper bound. Every ℳ ∈ 𝔐 lat \mathcal{M}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{lat}} and every n ≥ 2 n\geq 2 satisfy 𝔼 ℳ TV ( P ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) , P ( ⋅ ∣ H n , Θ ) ) ≲ log ⁡ n / n . {\mathbb{E}}_{\mathcal{M}}\operatorname{TV}\!\left(P(\cdot\mid H_{n}),P(\cdot\mid H_{n},\Theta)\right)\lesssim\sqrt{\log n/n}. • Matching worst-case lower bound. If, in addition, H θ > 0 H_{\theta}>0 , p ¯ < 1 \underline{p}<1 , and L β > 1 L_{\beta}>1 , then for every sufficiently large n n , there is a model ℳ n ∈ 𝔐 lat \mathcal{M}_{n}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{lat}} for which inf Q ℳ n 𝔼 ℳ n TV ( Q ℳ n ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) , P ( ⋅ ∣ H n , Θ ) ) ≳ log ⁡ n / n , \inf_{Q^{\mathcal{M}_{n}}}{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathcal{M}_{n}}\operatorname{TV}\!\left(Q^{\mathcal{M}_{n}}(\cdot\mid H_{n}),P(\cdot\mid H_{n},\Theta)\right)\gtrsim\sqrt{\log n/n}, where the infimum is over prompt-only Borel probability kernels from ℋ n {\mathcal{H}}_{n} to 𝒵 {\mathcal{Z}} that may know ℳ n \mathcal{M}_{n} . Posterior prediction makes oracle use of the prompt. The lower bound is an information limit: it remains valid with arbitrarily many independent pretraining episodes and unrestricted computation at generation time. For each fixed task family and prior, the posterior predictive has expected task-conditional TV risk at most twice that of the best prompt-only generator (see 156 ), implying it is an oracle prompt-only generator up to a constant factor. What matters is uncertainty about the output distribution, not the task label alone. Distinct tasks cause no generation error when they induce the same output distribution, while multimodality within a task should remain. The controlled experiment in Appendix J illustrates the posterior-predictive behavior: the generated distribution is broadly bimodal under a short, ambiguous context and contracts toward a narrow, essentially unimodal distribution as the context grows. Sharpness in a rich latent-task class. Fixed latent dimension still allows many weakly separated output distributions. The matching lower bound embeds about log ⁡ n \log n weakly distinguishable changes along a single latent coordinate, showing that the logarithmic factor reflects the richness of the task class. This is a worst-case result: the hard family and prior may depend on n n . A fixed family may have a faster rate or zero uncertainty.

sections.heading: 3.3 The minimax-optimal rate with a pretrained DiT
sections.text: Reaching the known-model rate from data. Section 3.2 grants the oracle generator the task family and prior. The DiT learning rule receives neither and observes no task labels. Yet Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 together give the same worst-case prompt-length rate. Corollary 3.3 (Task-conditional generation at the sharp prompt rate; informal version of Corollary H.4 ) . For sufficiently large n n , set ε = log ⁡ n / n \varepsilon=\sqrt{\log n/n} , use the score class and estimator of Theorem 3.1 with ε opt ≲ log ⁡ n / n \varepsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}\lesssim\log n/n , and let N N and M M satisfy 10 at this value of ε \varepsilon . For every fixed ℳ ∈ 𝔐 lat \mathcal{M}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{lat}} and δ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \delta\in(0,1) , with probability at least 1 − δ 1-\delta over pretraining and its diffusion augmentations, 𝔼 TV ( P ^ 0 | H n ( M ) , P ( ⋅ ∣ H n , Θ ) ) ≲ log ⁡ n n . {\mathbb{E}}\operatorname{TV}\!\left(\widehat{P}^{(M)}_{0\mid H_{n}},P(\cdot\mid H_{n},\Theta)\right)\lesssim\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}. (14) Here the expectation is over a fresh test episode conditional on the completed training run. Matching learning and sampling accuracy to prompt information. Pretraining episodes estimate the shared prompt-to-distribution rule, model capacity controls its approximation, and diffusion steps control sampling accuracy. Additional demonstrations instead provide more information about the fresh task. Keeping the learning and sampling errors at 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ n / n ) {\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{\log n/n}) lets the DiT attain the optimal rate for test-time generation. A geometric view of in-context generation. Assumption 3.1 defines a Hölder-parameterized family of task distributions. A finite prompt induces a posterior over this family, and the posterior predictive is the corresponding posterior-weighted barycenter of the distributions, which need not itself belong to the family (see Example I.1 , where task densities lie on a circle, while the posterior predictive can lie in its interior). In our finite representation, attention realizes this geometry by assigning posterior weights to representative tasks, so that its softmax weights can be viewed as barycentric weights over the latent task family. The same low-dimensional regularity controls statistical complexity: only polynomially many representative tasks are needed to approximate the predictive score, while the cumulative information about the latent task grows only logarithmically with the prompt length. This yields the 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ n / n ) {\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{\log n/n}) convergence of the posterior predictive toward the realized task distribution in expected total variation.

sections.heading: 4 Conclusion and Discussion
sections.text: We established finite-sample guarantees for posterior-predictive generation with a pretrained DiT, separating learning and sampling errors from finite-prompt task uncertainty. Under our assumptions, sufficient model capacity, pretraining data, optimization accuracy, and sampling resources yield the minimax-optimal prompt-length rate in task-conditional total variation. Preserving uncertainty is part of generative accuracy. A finite prompt may leave several task hypotheses plausible, so multimodality may be appropriate and mode collapse may constitute error ( Kohl et al., 2018 , cf.) . A sharper output distribution should not automatically count as improved quality. • As an architectural implication, because the posterior predictive need not contract to any single task distribution, our results motivate soft representations of plausible tasks without mandatory commitment like hard routing or switching ( Fedus et al., 2022 ) . • Our theory naturally raises a future research question: how to modify the test-time distribution? Guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ; Fu et al., 2024 ) , reward-based reranking or best-of- K K selection ( Amini et al., 2025 ) can improve sample utility while changing the probability mass assigned to plausible alternatives. How to improve utility while preserving, or explicitly controlling departures from, posterior-predictive calibration remains an open direction for in-context generation. Resource allocation should follow the source of uncertainty. Once learning and sampling errors are small relative to prompt uncertainty, additional diffusion steps cannot supply the missing task information. If the remaining multimodality reflects ambiguity between tasks, requesting another informative demonstration may therefore be more useful, motivating an extension to active demonstration acquisition ( Rainforth et al., 2024 ) . For pretraining, our generalization analysis counts independent episodes: observations within an episode share a latent task and are generally dependent. Total token count alone consequently does not characterize the effective training sample size. The appendix summarizes the corresponding bottlenecks and interventions.

sections.heading: Appendix A Additional Related Work
sections.text: Section 1.1 reviews the closely related work on ICL and Transformer-based score estimation. Here, we highlight the two diffusion-specific ingredients needed for our end-to-end analysis: learning a prompt-conditioned score from finitely many independent pretraining episodes, and separating posterior-predictive approximation error from the uncertainty that remains with a finite prompt. Diffusion-model theory commonly separates score estimation from the stability and discretization analysis of the reverse-time process. Score-to-sampling results translate suitable L 2 L^{2} score errors along the forward marginals into distributional sampling guarantees under various moment and regularity conditions ( Chen et al., 2023c ; Benton et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023a ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Complementary minimax analyses ask whether empirical score matching followed by reverse diffusion estimates a fixed data distribution at an optimal statistical rate ( Oko et al., 2023 ; Wibisono et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2023b ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Fu and Lee, 2025 ) . Related work also exploits structural or manifold assumptions to obtain generalization, convergence, or intrinsic-dimensional guarantees ( Yakovlev and Puchkin, 2025 ; Tang and Yang, 2024 ; Azangulov et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2026 ) . Our analysis uses the same broad score-to-distribution interface, but its input is the integrated prompt-conditioned risk of a score estimator learned from independent pretraining episodes. The randomly shifted inverse-variance time grid converts this integrated-in-time control into an expected total-variation guarantee for a finite-step reverse sampler, without requiring a score-error bound that holds uniformly over time. Conditional diffusion theory typically studies families of distributions indexed by an observed covariate ( Fu et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) , including approximation and estimation guarantees for conditional DiTs ( Hu et al., 2025 ) . In our episodic model, by contrast, the conditioning object is a random prompt H n H_{n} generated from an unobserved task. The prompt provides evidence about the latent task but does not directly index a single realized-task distribution. Consequently, the posterior-predictive distribution P ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) P(\cdot\mid H_{n}) is the score-learning target, while its discrepancy from the realized-task distribution P ( ⋅ ∣ H n , Θ ) P(\cdot\mid H_{n},\Theta) is analyzed separately as finite-prompt task uncertainty. Under the stated nondegeneracy conditions, our minimax prompt-length lower bound quantifies the unavoidable finite-prompt contribution to task-conditional total-variation risk.

sections.heading: Appendix B Formal Setup and Conventions
sections.text: Section 2 defines the episodic problem, the sample-only and input–output prompt models, evaluation distributions, and error decomposition. This appendix fixes the formal conventions used throughout the proofs. It proceeds from probability metrics and regular conditioning to the two latent-task prompt models, then specifies independent-episode pretraining and test-time generation, and finally records the Hölder classes used in the regularity assumptions.

sections.heading: Appendix D Latent-Task Regularity and Episode-KL Approximation
sections.text: The score representation in Appendix C averages over a continuous latent task space. This appendix prepares its finite approximation in four steps: compact preprocessing and tail control; likelihood and conditional-density regularity; normalized diffusion features and latent-grid quadrature; and an episode-level KL comparison that yields integrated score error under the true prompt law. Appendix E then approximates the resulting finite-mixture score with neural component maps and an exact four-block attention aggregation. Unless displayed explicitly, dependence on the fixed diffusion window ( t 0 , T ) (t_{0},T) and deterministic state radius R state , n R_{\mathrm{state},n} is suppressed.

sections.heading: Appendix E Transformer Construction, Approximation, and Class Complexity
sections.text: The finite latent average from Appendix D specifies the score computation to approximate. This section proceeds in three stages: it first defines the scaled-score metric and the prompt-conditioned Transformer class, then uses four attention blocks to aggregate the approximated finite-mixture components exactly, and finally derives the integrated approximation and class-complexity bounds. The last stage is needed because training need not return the specifically constructed parameters.

sections.text: For d , m ∈ ℕ d,m\in\mathbb{N} and a query token v ∈ ℝ d v\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} , key–value tokens x 1 , … , x m ∈ ℝ d x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} , and matrices W Q , W K , W V , W O ∈ ℝ d × d W_{Q},W_{K},W_{V},W_{O}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d\times d} , define the attention block ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) Att W Q , W K , W V , W O ( v ; x 1 : m ) := W O ∑ j = 1 m π j W V x j , π j := exp ⁡ { ( W Q ​ v ) ⊤ ​ W K ​ x j / d } ∑ k = 1 m exp ⁡ { ( W Q ​ v ) ⊤ ​ W K ​ x k / d } . \operatorname{Att}_{W_{Q},W_{K},W_{V},W_{O}}(v;x_{1:m}):=W_{O}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\pi_{j}W_{V}x_{j},\qquad\pi_{j}:=\frac{\exp\{(W_{Q}v)^{\top}W_{K}x_{j}/\sqrt{d}\}}{\sum_{k=1}^{m}\exp\{(W_{Q}v)^{\top}W_{K}x_{k}/\sqrt{d}\}}. Lemma E.2 (Sensitivity of scaled dot-product attention) . Fix B ≥ 1 B\geq 1 . Suppose every entry of the tokens and matrices in this attention map and in a primed copy is bounded in absolute value by B B . Let η att \eta_{\mathrm{att}} be the maximum of the entrywise matrix differences and the ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} distances between corresponding tokens. The bound is independent of the number of keys m m and remains valid after restricting both maps by the same deterministic nonempty attention mask. The proof follows the standard perturbation argument used in self-attention stability analyses ( Edelman et al., 2022 ; Takakura and Suzuki, 2023 ) ; we give the details because our version jointly perturbs the tokens and all four attention projections and must remain uniform in the number of masked keys. Proof. The matrix inequality ‖ A ​ x ‖ ∞ ≤ d ​ ‖ A ‖ max ​ ‖ x ‖ ∞ \|Ax\|_{\infty}\leq d\|A\|_{\max}\|x\|_{\infty} gives ‖ W Q ​ v − W Q ′ ​ v ′ ‖ ∞ + max j ⁡ ‖ W K ​ x j − W K ′ ​ x j ′ ‖ ∞ ≤ 4 ​ d ​ B ​ η att . \|W_{Q}v-W^{\prime}_{Q}v^{\prime}\|_{\infty}+\max_{j}\|W_{K}x_{j}-W^{\prime}_{K}x_{j}^{\prime}\|_{\infty}\leq 4dB\eta_{\mathrm{att}}. sections.heading: Appendix F Pretraining and Score Learning from Independent Episodes
sections.text: This section turns the approximation class from Appendix E into a finite-episode learning guarantee. We first define clipped variance-balanced DSM and its population target, then establish uniform convergence in the scaled-score metric, and finally combine approximation, clipping, optimization, covering, and estimation errors for the Transformer class.

sections.heading: F.1 Clipped Labels and the Empirical bDSM Objective
sections.text: The training sample consists of N N independent episodes, each augmented with one independent diffusion time and Gaussian perturbation. Bounding the scaled-score output and clipping the Gaussian label yield a bounded squared loss. The resulting theorem separates approximation, clipping, optimization, covering, and estimation errors.

sections.heading: F.4 Error Decomposition and Tuning Guidance
sections.text: The first three terms in 112 measure model approximation, label clipping, and optimization. The final two arise from the uniform-convergence argument: one accounts for extending the bound from a finite cover to the entire score class, and the other is the covering-number generalization term. Only these final two terms depend on the cover radius, and the generalization term also depends logarithmically on the cover cardinality. sections.heading: Appendix G Reverse Diffusion Sampling and Posterior-Predictive Generation
sections.text: This section converts integrated score error into a posterior-predictive generation guarantee. We first define the randomized inverse-variance time grid and establish the exact reverse-process and endpoint estimates. We then combine a finite-energy KL comparison with exact-score dynamics to obtain a positive-time discretization bound. The final four subsections choose the accuracy parameters and tail radii, combine approximation, learning, and sampling, and record the scalar sample-only specialization. The finite-step theorem applies, conditionally on training, to any finite-valued jointly Borel score with finite integrated score error; its output law averages over the independent grid shift and Gaussian sampling noise. Throughout, M ∈ ℕ M\in\mathbb{N} is the number, or an almost-sure upper bound on the number, of reverse updates. A small time-integrated error does not ensure accuracy at predetermined evaluation times for a merely measurable score. The randomized grid in Section 2.4 addresses this mismatch: averaging the variance-weighted sum of score errors over its shift recovers the training integral. This makes the score-learning guarantee applicable to the sampler without an additional time-regularity assumption. Corollary G.6 bounds predictive error by initialization, the square root of integrated score error, early stopping, and discretization. The bound concerns the sampler’s output distribution averaged over its independent grid shift and uses at most M M score evaluations almost surely under 136 .

sections.text: Recall the conditional OU marginals and score from Section C.1 . Let r ∈ [ 0 , T ) r\in[0,T) be increasing reverse time, so that the corresponding forward time is t = T − r t=T-r . sections.heading: Appendix H Sharp Finite-Prompt Task Uncertainty
sections.text: This appendix first states the finite-prompt uncertainty theorem, then proves it in three steps: posterior averaging compares task uncertainty with oracle risk, predictive information gives the upper bound, and an Assouad construction gives the matching lower bound. The final subsection combines this result with Theorem 3.1 to obtain the task-conditional guarantee. The input–output argument keeps the fresh query in the conditioning variables, and the family used for the lower bound varies along only one latent coordinate while the class bounds remain fixed.

sections.heading: H.1 Finite-Prompt Theorem and Oracle Risk
sections.text: Even exact posterior prediction can differ from the realized task distribution. We therefore quantify this difference over the model class 𝔐 lat \mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{lat}} defined after Assumption 3.1 , whose members share the same dimensions and regularity bounds. For each ℳ \mathcal{M} , the symbols Pr ℳ \Pr_{\mathcal{M}} , 𝔼 ℳ {\mathbb{E}}_{\mathcal{M}} , and 𝖫𝖺𝗐 ℳ \mathsf{Law}_{\mathcal{M}} refer to its induced joint law; the dependence of the kernels P P on ℳ \mathcal{M} is suppressed. For a known model ℳ ∈ 𝔐 lat \mathcal{M}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{lat}} , define the oracle task risk ℛ n or ( ℳ ) := inf Q ℳ 𝔼 ℳ 𝖳𝖵 ( Q ℳ ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) , P ( ⋅ ∣ H n , Θ ) ) , \mathcal{R}_{n}^{\mathrm{or}}(\mathcal{M}):=\inf_{Q^{\mathcal{M}}}{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathcal{M}}{\mathsf{TV}}\bigl(Q^{\mathcal{M}}(\cdot\mid H_{n}),P(\cdot\mid H_{n},\Theta)\bigr), (155) where the infimum is over Borel probability kernels from ℋ n {\mathcal{H}}_{n} to 𝒵 {\mathcal{Z}} that may use the entire task family and task prior. Generation randomness is included in the output distribution. An independent random seed cannot improve the infimum by convexity of TV. Lemma H.2 and the Borel posterior-predictive kernel fixed in 16 imply ℛ n or ( ℳ ) ≤ 𝔼 ℳ 𝖳𝖵 ( P ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) , P ( ⋅ ∣ H n , Θ ) ) ≤ 2 ℛ n or ( ℳ ) . \mathcal{R}_{n}^{\mathrm{or}}(\mathcal{M})\leq{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathcal{M}}{\mathsf{TV}}\!\bigl(P(\cdot\mid H_{n}),P(\cdot\mid H_{n},\Theta)\bigr)\leq 2\mathcal{R}_{n}^{\mathrm{or}}(\mathcal{M}). (156) A lower bound on this oracle risk therefore limits every generator, including one with unlimited independent pretraining. Theorem H.1 (Uniform upper and matching lower bounds for finite-prompt task uncertainty) . Uniform upper bound. For every ℳ ∈ 𝔐 lat \mathcal{M}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{lat}} and n ≥ 1 n\geq 1 , the following bound holds with an implicit constant depending only on the common class parameters: 𝔼 ℳ KL ( P ( ⋅ ∣ H n , Θ ) ∥ P ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) ) ≲ log ⁡ ( e ​ n ) n . {\mathbb{E}}_{\mathcal{M}}\mathrm{KL}\!\bigl(P(\cdot\mid H_{n},\Theta)\,\|\,P(\cdot\mid H_{n})\bigr)\lesssim\frac{\log(en)}{n}. (157) Consequently, 𝔼 ℳ 𝖳𝖵 ( P ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) , P ( ⋅ ∣ H n , Θ ) ) ≲ log ⁡ ( e ​ n ) n {\mathbb{E}}_{\mathcal{M}}{\mathsf{TV}}\!\bigl(P(\cdot\mid H_{n}),P(\cdot\mid H_{n},\Theta)\bigr)\lesssim\sqrt{\frac{\log(en)}{n}} uniformly over ℳ ∈ 𝔐 lat \mathcal{M}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{lat}} . Matching lower bound. If H θ > 0 H_{\theta}>0 , p ¯ < 1 \underline{p}<1 , and L β > 1 L_{\beta}>1 , then, for all sufficiently large n n , log ⁡ ( e ​ n ) n \displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{\log(en)}{n}} ≲ sup ℳ ∈ 𝔐 lat ℛ n or ​ ( ℳ ) \displaystyle\lesssim\sup_{\mathcal{M}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{lat}}}\mathcal{R}_{n}^{\mathrm{or}}(\mathcal{M}) (158) ≤ sup ℳ ∈ 𝔐 lat 𝔼 ℳ 𝖳𝖵 ( P ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) , P ( ⋅ ∣ H n , Θ ) ) ≲ log ⁡ ( e ​ n ) n . \displaystyle\leq\sup_{\mathcal{M}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{lat}}}{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathcal{M}}{\mathsf{TV}}\!\bigl(P(\cdot\mid H_{n}),P(\cdot\mid H_{n},\Theta)\bigr)\lesssim\sqrt{\frac{\log(en)}{n}}. The lower bound allows any number of independent training episodes, including a countably infinite sequence, and unrestricted computation at generation time. The implicit constants and the sufficiently-large- n n threshold depend only on the common class parameters. The worst-case model and prior may depend on n n , while all class parameters remain fixed. Asymptotic interpretation of the upper bound. The uniform upper bound gives 𝔼 ℳ 𝖳𝖵 ( P ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) , P ( ⋅ ∣ H n , Θ ) ) ≲ log ⁡ ( e ​ n ) / n . {\mathbb{E}}_{\mathcal{M}}{\mathsf{TV}}\!\bigl(P(\cdot\mid H_{n}),P(\cdot\mid H_{n},\Theta)\bigr)\lesssim\sqrt{\log(en)/n}. Thus the expected TV error tends to zero. In particular, for every fixed ρ TV > 0 \rho_{\mathrm{TV}}>0 , Markov’s inequality gives Pr ℳ ( 𝖳𝖵 ( P ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) , P ( ⋅ ∣ H n , Θ ) ) > ρ TV ) \displaystyle\Pr_{\mathcal{M}}\bigl({\mathsf{TV}}\!\bigl(P(\cdot\mid H_{n}),P(\cdot\mid H_{n},\Theta)\bigr)>\rho_{\mathrm{TV}}\bigr) ≤ 1 ρ TV 𝔼 ℳ 𝖳𝖵 ( P ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) , P ( ⋅ ∣ H n , Θ ) ) ≲ 1 ρ TV log ⁡ ( e ​ n ) n . \displaystyle\qquad\leq\frac{1}{\rho_{\mathrm{TV}}}{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathcal{M}}{\mathsf{TV}}\!\bigl(P(\cdot\mid H_{n}),P(\cdot\mid H_{n},\Theta)\bigr)\lesssim\frac{1}{\rho_{\mathrm{TV}}}\sqrt{\frac{\log(en)}{n}}. Hence the TV error converges to zero in probability under the joint law of the realized task and prompt for each fixed ℳ \mathcal{M} . This is convergence of the posterior-predictive output distribution to the realized task-conditional output distribution. It does not establish convergence for every fixed θ \theta , almost-sure convergence, or contraction of Π ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) \Pi(\cdot\mid H_{n}) to δ Θ \delta_{\Theta} . Recovery of a unique latent parameter would additionally require identifiability; predictive convergence itself does not, since different parameters may induce the same distribution. The upper bound applies to every ℳ ∈ 𝔐 lat \mathcal{M}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\mathrm{lat}} without the additional nondegeneracy conditions. The matching lower bound shows that the upper bound’s dependence on n n cannot be improved uniformly over the stated nondegenerate class, even when the family and prior are known; it does not assert that every fixed family or prior attains this rate. The predictive KL upper bound is proved in Section H.3 , and the matching lower bound is proved in Section H.4 .

sections.heading: H.2 Posterior Averaging and Oracle Comparison
sections.text: The posterior-predictive distribution averages the task law conditional on the prompt. The following lemma bounds its expected task-conditional TV error by twice that of any prompt-based probability kernel. Lemma H.2 (Posterior averaging bound) . Suppose the posterior-mixture identity in 2 holds, and let h ↦ Q ( ⋅ | h ) h\mapsto Q(\cdot\,|\,h) be any measurable probability kernel from ℋ n {\mathcal{H}}_{n} to 𝒵 {\mathcal{Z}} . Then 𝔼 [ 𝖳𝖵 ( P ( ⋅ | H n ) , P ( ⋅ | H n , Θ ) ) ] ≤ 2 𝔼 [ 𝖳𝖵 ( Q ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) , P ( ⋅ | H n , Θ ) ) ] . {\mathbb{E}}\left[{\mathsf{TV}}\!\left(P(\cdot\,|\,H_{n}),P(\cdot\,|\,H_{n},\Theta)\right)\right]\leq 2{\mathbb{E}}\left[{\mathsf{TV}}\!\left(Q(\cdot\mid H_{n}),P(\cdot\,|\,H_{n},\Theta)\right)\right]. Proof. Write Q h = Q ( ⋅ ∣ h ) Q_{h}=Q(\cdot\mid h) and R h , θ = P ( ⋅ ∣ h , θ ) R_{h,\theta}=P(\cdot\mid h,\theta) . On the common full-measure set where the posterior-mixture identity holds, convexity of TV gives 𝖳𝖵 ( Q h , P ( ⋅ ∣ h ) ) ≤ ∫ 𝖳𝖵 ( Q h , R h , θ ) Π ( d θ ∣ h ) . {\mathsf{TV}}(Q_{h},P(\cdot\mid h))\leq\int{\mathsf{TV}}(Q_{h},R_{h,\theta})\Pi({\mathrm{d}}\theta\mid h). These TV distances are measurable and bounded by one: on a standard Borel space, the defining supremum can be taken over a countable generating algebra. Taking expectations and applying the tower property yields 𝔼 𝖳𝖵 ( Q ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) , P ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) ) ≤ 𝔼 𝖳𝖵 ( Q ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) , P ( ⋅ ∣ H n , Θ ) ) . {\mathbb{E}}{\mathsf{TV}}(Q(\cdot\mid H_{n}),P(\cdot\mid H_{n}))\leq{\mathbb{E}}{\mathsf{TV}}(Q(\cdot\mid H_{n}),P(\cdot\mid H_{n},\Theta)). The triangle inequality through Q ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) Q(\cdot\mid H_{n}) proves the claim. ∎ The lemma uses only the posterior-mixture identity in 2 and the measurability of Q ( ⋅ ∣ H n ) Q(\cdot\mid H_{n}) as a function of the prompt. The TV bound requires no density, smoothness, conditional i.i.d., or diffusion assumption. Taking the infimum over Q Q gives the factor-two oracle comparison in 156 ; the reverse inequality follows by choosing the posterior-predictive kernel. Under TV loss, the posterior-predictive distribution need not minimize posterior expected TV loss: with posterior weights 0.9 0.9 and 0.1 0.1 on δ 0 \delta_{0} and δ 1 \delta_{1} , its posterior expected loss is 0.18 0.18 , whereas δ 0 \delta_{0} has loss 0.1 0.1 . Thus, Lemma H.2 is a factor-two posterior-averaging bound, not an exact Bayes-optimality statement.

sections.heading: J.1 Posterior-Predictive Generation in a Synthetic Image Task
sections.text: To illustrate the distributional behavior motivated by our theory, we construct a synthetic episodic image-transformation task with an exact, generally bimodal posterior-predictive distribution. The task is designed so that a short context leaves the sign of a latent transformation rule ambiguous, whereas a longer context identifies the sign and contracts the query distribution. We use the experiment to ask whether a diffusion Transformer can represent both modes under an ambiguous context, contract toward the appropriate mode as more demonstrations are observed, and learn this prompt-to-distribution map from increasing numbers of pretraining episodes while preserving the query content. Following controlled synthetic experiments in previous ICL studies ( Panwar et al., 2024 ; Wakayama and Suzuki, 2026 ; Ma et al., 2025 , e.g.,) , we use a simple task family in which the latent rule and its posterior predictive can be calculated exactly.

sections.heading: J.1.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Each episode has a shared binary latent variable G ∈ { − 1 , + 1 } , Pr ⁡ ( G = − 1 ) = Pr ⁡ ( G = + 1 ) = 1 2 . G\in\{-1,+1\},\qquad\Pr(G=-1)=\Pr(G=+1)=\frac{1}{2}. We train a cross-attention DiT ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) on this episodic task. Each context pair ( X i , Y i ) (X_{i},Y_{i}) is concatenated along the channel dimension and mapped by a convolutional pair encoder to a 2 × 2 2\times 2 grid of four 512 512 -dimensional tokens. The hidden dimension is 512 512 , the number of attention heads is 8 8 , the feed-forward dimension is 2,048 2{,}048 , and the model has 80,271,180 80{,}271{,}180 trainable parameters. sections.heading: J.1.2 Results
sections.text: We first examine the effect of the number of training episodes. Fig. 3 evaluates checkpoints at 5,000 5{,}000 , 10,000 10{,}000 , 20,000 20{,}000 , 30,000 30{,}000 , and 40,000 40{,}000 optimizer updates, corresponding to N ∈ { 0.32 , 0.64 , 1.28 , 1.92 , 2.56 } N\in\{0.32,0.64,1.28,1.92,2.56\} million episodes. The same 64 64 fixed test tasks are evaluated at context length n = 64 n=64 with 256 256 generations per task using the raw weights. As N N increases, the mean right-probability error decreases from 0.448 0.448 to 0.016 0.016 , and position W 1 W_{1} decreases from 0.252 0.252 to 0.041 0.041 . Both distributional metrics improve most sharply between 0.64 0.64 and 1.28 1.28 million episodes. In contrast, aligned content IoU remains approximately 0.83 0.83 – 0.85 0.85 throughout training. Thus, the model learns to render and preserve the query object early, while additional episodes primarily improve inference of the latent rule and calibration of the posterior-predictive position distribution. Figure 3: Scaling with the number of training episodes. Performance at 0.32 0.32 , 0.64 0.64 , 1.28 1.28 , 1.92 1.92 , and 2.56 2.56 million episodes. From left to right, the panels show the right-probability error, the 1 1 -Wasserstein distance between the recovered generated-position distribution and the exact two-component Gaussian posterior predictive, and aligned content IoU. Evaluation uses the same 64 64 fixed test tasks, n = 64 n=64 , 256 256 generations per task, and the raw model weights. Error bars indicate the standard error across tasks. We next study test-time scaling with the context length. Fig. 4 shows the recovered position distribution for a representative fixed task (task 12) under nested contexts of lengths n ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } n\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\} . At n = 1 n=1 , the sign of the latent slope is not identified, and both the exact posterior predictive and the model distribution have left and right modes. As more examples are observed, the posterior probability over the slope sign concentrates and the exact distribution contracts toward the left mode. The model reproduces this overall transition, but contraction is delayed in the intermediate regime. In particular, at n = 8 n=8 , the exact posterior predictive has already placed almost all of its mass on the left mode, whereas the model still assigns visible probability mass to the right mode. By n = 16 n=16 , the generated distribution is narrow and essentially unimodal, closely matching the exact posterior predictive, and the agreement persists at larger context lengths. Because the panels follow one realized episode, newly observed noise can transiently change the posterior mode probabilities, so the degree of concentration need not evolve monotonically at every intermediate context length. Figure 4: Posterior-predictive contraction with context length. Each column corresponds to n ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } n\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\} for the same fixed task and query. Histograms show positions recovered from 256 256 generated images using the raw model weights, and green curves show the analytically exact posterior-predictive distribution. The dotted line at c = 0.5 c=0.5 separates the left and right modes. The model captures the transition from a broad bimodal predictive law at short contexts to a narrow, essentially unimodal law at long contexts, with visible excess right-mode mass in the intermediate regime. Finally, Fig. 5 gives qualitative examples of posterior-predictive generation for a circle query and a triangle query, comparing n = 1 n=1 and n = 8 n=8 with the raw weights. For the circle task, the exact right-mode probability changes from 0.550 0.550 to 0.999 0.999 , while the generated frequency changes from 0.562 0.562 to 0.965 0.965 . For the triangle task, the exact right-mode probability instead changes from 0.527 0.527 to 0.009 0.009 , while the generated frequency changes from 0.410 0.410 to 0.055 0.055 . Thus, a short context leaves both horizontal placements plausible, whereas the longer context selects the right mode for the circle and the left mode for the triangle. The individual generations preserve the query shape in both cases. The pixel averages at n = 1 n=1 are blurred along the horizontal direction because they combine samples from both modes, whereas the averages at n = 8 n=8 are sharp after the posterior predictive has concentrated. A single averaged image obscures the multimodal uncertainty represented by the generated sample distribution. Figure 5: Qualitative posterior-predictive generation. The top half shows a task with a circle query, and the bottom half shows a task with a triangle query; each task is displayed at n = 1 n=1 and n = 8 n=8 . From left to right, each row contains the available context input–output pairs X i → Y i X_{i}\to Y_{i} , the untransformed query input, four independent generations for that query, and the pixel-wise average of 256 256 generations. All samples use the raw model weights. For the circle task, the exact/generated right-mode probabilities are 0.550 / 0.562 0.550/0.562 at n = 1 n=1 and 0.999 / 0.965 0.999/0.965 at n = 8 n=8 . For the other task, they are 0.527 / 0.410 0.527/0.410 at n = 1 n=1 and 0.009 / 0.055 0.009/0.055 at n = 8 n=8 . The horizontally blurred averages at n = 1 n=1 reflect bimodality, while the sharp averages at n = 8 n=8 reflect posterior-predictive contraction.

sections.heading: J.2 Oracle Diagnostics for Predictive and Task-Conditional Error
sections.text: The image experiment above evaluates posterior-predictive learning in a trained diffusion model. We next complement it with a separate oracle diagnostic in a simple known-density family, isolating task uncertainty from predictive approximation without neural training or reverse sampling.

sections.heading: J.2.1 Task uncertainty and predictive approximation in a known family
sections.text: The two error targets can be seen in a sample-only family with known densities and prior: g θ ​ ( z ) = 1 + 1 4 ​ cos ⁡ ( 2 ​ π ​ ( z − θ ) ) g_{\theta}(z)=1+\tfrac{1}{4}\cos(2\pi(z-\theta)) for z , θ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] z,\theta\in[0,1] , with Π = Unif ⁡ [ 0 , 1 ] \Pi=\mathrm{Unif}[0,1] . This positive sinusoidal family satisfies the task assumptions ( Example I.1 ). We compute its exact predictive density and compare it with both the realized task density and a predictive approximation on a finite latent grid. This fixed-family diagnostic does not test the worst-case rate, neural training, or reverse sampling. In Figure 6 , longer prompts reduce the observed mean task uncertainty. At fixed prompt length, a finer grid instead reduces error against the posterior predictive. These are distinct effects: the former uses more examples from the task, while the latter refines the calculation on the same prompt. The calculations below give the analytical TV formulas, quadrature checks, seeds, and recorded per-episode results.

sections.heading: Appendix K Qualitative Diagnostics and Resource Allocation
sections.text: The decomposition in Section 2.2 separates posterior-predictive generation error from finite-prompt task uncertainty. Table 2 translates this decomposition into qualitative diagnostics for experiments and resource allocation. The entries are not mutually exclusive and should be interpreted as diagnostic hypotheses rather than as additional theorem statements. Table 2: Qualitative diagnostics and resource allocation for in-context generation. Observed pattern Possible bottleneck Suggested intervention The task posterior remains spread over tasks with different output laws. Finite-prompt task uncertainty Request additional demonstrations that distinguish the plausible task-specific output laws. The oracle is concentrated, but the model remains diffuse after checking sampler convergence. Amortization or learning error Increase independent pretraining episodes; improve model capacity, optimization, or use of context. Error relative to the oracle varies substantially with sampler steps or schedule. Sampling error or score–sampler interaction Refine the sampler steps and schedule; check convergence with the learned score held fixed. Individual samples are plausible, but their mode frequencies disagree with the oracle. Probability calibration error Evaluate mode probabilities, improve episodic distributional training, and check sensitivity to the sampler. Learning and sampling errors are small relative to finite-prompt task uncertainty. Prompt information Prioritize more informative demonstrations over further reductions in learning or sampling error. A large token budget contains few independent episodes. Limited independent training data Track and increase independent episode count; account for within-episode dependence when allocating pretraining data.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.05333v1 [cs.LG] 04 Oct 2026 Diffusion Transformers are Provably Optimal In-context Generators Guoji Fu National University of Singapore Singapore guoji.fu@u.nus.edu Tomoya Wakayama RIKEN AIP Tokyo, Japan tomoya.wakayama@riken.jp Ryotaro Kawata The University of Tokyo Tokyo, Japan kawata-ryotaro725@g.ecc.u-tokyo.ac.jp Atsushi Nitanda A*STAR CFAR Nanyang Technological University Singapore atsushi_nitanda@a-star.edu.sg Wee Sun Lee National University of Singapore Singapore leews@comp.nus.edu.sg Taiji Suzuki The University of Tokyo RIKEN AIP Tokyo, Japan taiji@mist.i.u-tokyo.ac.jp Abstract Generative foundation models are attracting interest for their ability to produce desired outputs from demonstrations given at inference time, without updating parameters. However, since a few demonstrations cannot uniquely identify the intended task, the challenge is how to learn and sample from an output distribution that reflects this task uncertainty. In this work, we theoretically analyze how a Diffusion Transformer (DiT), pretrained across diverse tasks, learns and generates predictive distributions for a new query from demonstrations. We first show that the natural target to generate from finite demonstrations is not an output derived from estimating a single task, but rather a predictive distribution that captures the task uncertainty remaining after observing the demonstrations. We then prove that a DiT can learn this predictive distribution through score estimation, using attention to aggregate information from demonstrations and diffusion to generate samples. Owing to this property, with sufficient pretraining resources and diffusion sampling steps, the resulting DiT achieves the minimax optimal rate over a Hölder class of test-time tasks. These results imply that DiT acts as a statistically grounded in-context generator capable of generating distributions adapted to new tasks while retaining the uncertainty inherent in finite demonstrations. 1 Introduction Generative models have advanced rapidly over the past few years with diffusion models in particular achieving remarkable success in synthesizing complex high-dimensional data such as images ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Chi et al., 2023 ) . At the same time, in-context learning (ICL) has shown that a pretrained model can adapt to a new task from a few demonstrations without updating its parameters ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Dong et al., 2024 ) . These developments motivate in-context generation : using demonstrations to specify what kinds of outputs should be generated for a new query ( Bar et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) . Fig. 1 illustrates this idea in a robotic manipulation example: a user provides several examples of acceptable behaviors and asks the model to generate an appropriate action for a new object. More broadly, in image generation and other structured domains ( Fu et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) , the desired behavior may depend on visual, geometric, or stylistic criteria that are cumbersome to specify perfectly in natural language or mathematical form. In such cases, demonstrations serve as a natural interface for specifying what should be generated, and in-context generation is the mechanism that turns this interface into a working system. Yet demonstrations are not necessarily a complete specification of the underlying task. With only finitely many examples, multiple latent rules may remain compatible with the same context while implying different outputs for a new query, leaving uncertainty about what should be generated ( Xie et al., 2022 ; Panwar et al., 2024 ) . The output distribution that the context induces at a new query is then frequently non-degenerate or even multimodal. Collapsing this distribution to its mean can yield implausible outputs (Fig. 1 ; see also Blau and Michaeli, 2018 ; Chi et al., 2023 ). Selecting a single plausible candidate instead discards the relative probabilities of alternatives, preventing faithful reproduction of the distribution and potentially compromising downstream decision-making under uncertainty ( Kohl et al., 2018 ; Hoeting et al., 1999 ; Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ) . Thus, what in-context generation should deliver is not a single prediction but samples drawn from the predictive distribution itself, so that the uncertainty left by the finite demonstrations is preserved. Figure 1: In-context generation from demonstrations. A user specifies a desired behavior through a few examples rather than an explicit rule. Because a finite context may be consistent with multiple underlying rules, different outputs can remain plausible for the same query; collapsing the plausible outputs to a single average can produce an invalid result. Despite substantial theoretical progress on both in-context learning and diffusion models, existing frameworks do not cover this generative setting. Most finite-sample statistical analyses of ICL focus on point prediction under regression-type losses, studying how pretrained Transformers output optimal regression rules or Bayes predictors from a finite context ( Bai et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Wakayama and Suzuki, 2026 ) . In contrast, conditional generative modeling and conditional diffusion models aim to learn an entire output distribution given an observed covariate or conditioning variable ( Fu et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2025 ) . These settings typically assume that, at the population level, the observed condition indexes a well-defined conditional distribution. In-context generation is different: the condition itself is a finite collection of demonstrations generated from an unobserved task, and provides only partial information about the test distribution. Consequently, it remains unclear how a predictive distribution should be formed from finitely many demonstrations, and how a pretrained generative model can learn and sample from this distribution across tasks. In this paper, we formulate in-context generation as sampling from the distribution of outputs that remain plausible after finite demonstrations, rather than committing to a single inferred task or output. We identify this target with the posterior-predictive distribution and give a finite-sample theory of how a pretrained diffusion Transformer ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 , DiT;) learns the corresponding prompt-to-distribution map and realizes it through diffusion sampling. Our main findings are as follows. • Pretraining learns the shared rule; demonstrations reduce task uncertainty. We identify two distinct error sources: error from learning and sampling the shared prompt-to-distribution mapping, and the uncertainty left by the current prompt. More pretraining data and computation can reduce the former, but cannot in general eliminate the latter. • Attention infers; diffusion generates. Our construction shows that attention aggregates evidence from demonstrations into weights over plausible tasks, while diffusion converts the resulting predictive mixture into samples. With finite pretraining data and no task labels, a sufficiently large DiT and sampler can approximate the posterior-predictive distribution to any prescribed accuracy under our assumptions. • Minimax-optimal in-context generation via DiT. We establish matching upper and lower bounds for finite-prompt uncertainty and show that, over the nondegenerate Hölder task class, the learned DiT attains the minimax-optimal prompt-length rate log ⁡ n / n \sqrt{\log n/n} in task-conditional total-variation error, given sufficient model capacity, pretraining episodes, and diffusion steps. This demonstrates the test-time adaptive generation of DiT. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 defines the data-generating process and evaluation criteria, then introduces the DiT, its training objective, and its reverse sampler. Section 3 explains the task-family assumptions and the score-learning, prompt-uncertainty, and task-conditional generation guarantees, together with the main ideas behind their proofs. Section 4 presents a summary and practical implications. The appendices contain the proofs and empirical illustrations. 1.1 Related Work (A) ICL theory. Existing statistical theories of ICL primarily study point prediction, often under regression-type losses, and characterize how pretrained Transformers implement or approximate task-adaptive estimators ( Bai et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024b ; Kim et al., 2024 ) . Bayesian analyses further interpret ICL through posterior prediction over latent tasks ( Wakayama and Suzuki, 2026 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . Our focus is different: we study generation of the full posterior-predictive output distribution and its finite-sample error under distributional loss. Kang et al. (2026) give a constructive Transformer approximation of the posterior-predictive distribution in Gaussian-process (GP) regression. However, their theory assumes a known GP model with fixed kernel and noise parameters and does not establish generalization from finite pretraining data. By contrast, our result learns a prompt-conditioned diffusion score from finitely many independent pretraining examples without knowing the Hölder task family or task prior, and controls expected posterior-predictive TV error of the resulting finite-step reverse diffusion sampler. (B) Score learning with Transformers. Prior work shows Transformers can represent score estimators or denoising updates ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Smart et al., 2025 ; Rosu et al., 2025 ) ; Adibi et al. (2026) construct frozen Transformers simulating closed-form diffusion recursions and approximating an estimation-free empirical sampler. Our focus is statistical rather than merely representational: we analyze a DiT learned from finite pretraining data and show that finite-step reverse diffusion achieves posterior-predictive accuracy, achieving the minimax-optimal rate with respect to prompt length. Further related work on diffusion model theory is discussed in Appendix A . 2 In-Context Generation Setup and Diffusion Transformer We first specify the data-generating process and the two output distributions used to evaluate in-context generation.
